speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
maintopic: TABLING OF WHITE PAPER ON ANTI-DUMPING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to table, in English and in French, a copy of a white paper on antidumping. As hon. members are aware, to implement the anti-dumping code negotiated in the Kennedy round certain revisions are required to existing customs legislation. It is the government's intention to seek the approval of parliament in the near future for a separate statute dealing exclusively with the application of anti-dumping duties. The white paper is being made public at this time to provide hon. members and other interested parties with an opportunity to examine and comment on the kind of legislative provisions being contemplated to give effect to the antidumping code. I also suggest that the white paper be referred to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, as soon as the house agrees to set up this body.

maintopic: TABLING OF WHITE PAPER ON ANTI-DUMPING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short comment in this regard. It is particularly apposite that the white paper should be brought forward now. However, in view of the fact that recently the United States Senate passed a renegotiation bill which also contains provision for the repeal of the antidumping convention entered into by the United States, and as dumping affects Canada and the United States particularly, I think this house will want to examine this convention and the proposed legislation very carefully in light of events outside this country.

subtopic: TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON REFERENCE

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON REFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have tabled today copies in English and in French of the report of the tariff board on reference No. 134, together with a transcript of the evidence presented to the board at its public hearings.
Reference No. 134, equipment for hospitals and other institutions, covers items in the customs tariff which provide for the duty free entry of goods imported for hospitals, educational, scientific, religious and other institutions, and of goods imported for the benefit of afflicted or handicapped persons.
I assure the house that the board's recommendations will be considered carefully by the government. Interested parties who wish to comment on this report should do so as soon as possible.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the Prime Minister is leaving the chamber, I sent a message to his office this morning asking whether he would be good enough to remain in the chamber because I intend to refer to him a number of times in my speech, and I believe it is always fair to let a member know about this in advance. I have done so. However, if the Prime Minister decides that he is not able to remain in the chamber, that of course is his business.
During the election campaign and since we have heard a great deal about the just society. The Canadian people are now interested in knowing what steps the government intends to take so that Canada will become a more just society than it is today. I believe we in this chamber should ask ourselves what conditions should be corrected so that in Canada we may have a more just society than

September 20, 1968
The Address-Mr. Hees we have ever had before. I think all members of this house and all Canadians would agree that poverty is something which cannot be tolerated in any society which calls itself just. I believe the Prime Minister and all members of the Government would agree that a society that did not do its utmost to remove poverty from within its midst could not deem itself to be a just society.
In recent weeks, through reading the report of the Economic Council of Canada, we have learned a good deal about the question of poverty. The chapter devoted to this contains 37 pages. The question of poverty was dealt with in great detail. The report describes poverty in Canada today as a national disgrace. I was very interested to hear the Prime Minister agree with this opinion. He has said he agrees that poverty in Canada today is a national disgrace.
From this report we have learned a number of important things. We have learned first of all that there are 4,200,000 Canadians living in poverty in Canada at this very time. The report describes the conditions in which these
4,200,000	people are living in the following terms: the sour atmosphere of poor health, bad housing, accumulated defeat, alienation and despair, a sense of helplessness and entrapment. It says this is often disguised because it does not invariably go in rags and can pass unnoticed.
Second, the report tells us about the incomes received by the people of Canada who are living in conditions of poverty. It refers to single people earning less than $1,500 a year, married people with two children earning less than $2,500 a year, married people with three children earning less than $3,000 a year, married people with four children earning less than $3,500 a year and married people with five children earning less than $4,000 a year.
Third, we are told that poverty is not usually to be found only in those locations which we have learned to consider as depressed areas. It tells us that poverty is spread fairly evenly across this country. A great deal of it is found in the large metropolitan centres of the country which usually are considered to be affluent areas.
Fourth, we are told that the majority of the people who live in conditions of poverty today are not unemployed but are employed for the most part in the following industries: laundries, tanneries, lumber mills, clothing factories, hotels, restaurants, taverns, dry cleaning establishments, the retail trade, the
September 20, 1968

shoe industry, the box factories and woollen mills.
Fifth, we are told that most of these people who are suffering from poverty today are working for the minimum wages that are established by the federal government and the provincial governments for the industries which come under their jurisdiction. Those who have read the report are left with no doubt that the people who are suffering from poverty today will be raised from that condition only if these minimum wages are increased, and increased adequately now.
[DOT] (12 noon)
I should like to give hon. members an example of why these minimum wages should be increased at the present time. The minimum wage in respect of industry under federal jurisdiction was last raised on July 1, 1965 to $1.25 per hour. Since this increase the cost of living has risen by 12 per cent. I was not a member of the house when the last increase in the minimum wage in industries under federal jurisdiction came into effect but I assume that the members of the house who discussed this matter then satisfied themselves that a wage of $1.25 per hour was adequate to lift the people who receive such a wage out of the realm of poverty and above the poverty line. As the cost of living has increased by 12 per cent since that wage increase went into effect it is obvious that these wages are at least 12 per cent too low today. The same applies to wages which fall within provincial jurisdiction. These minimum wages vary across the country between $1 and $1.25 per hour and are as low as 80 cents an hour for women.
As we all know, those employees in Canada who come under union agreements have their wage agreements examined and negotiated with their employers usually every two years. These negotiations always result in substantial increases and increased fringe benefits, so those people who work in these industries are provided for adequately. That is the way it should be.
On the other hand, one-fifth of the workers across this country work for minimum wages and they do not have anyone to bargain for them. They have no one to go to their employers and demand an increase in wages to compensate for any increase in the cost of living. They have no one to negotiate the same type of health insurance plans and retirement plans that organized workers receive as a result of negotiations by their
The Address-Mr. Hees union representatives. This one-fifth of the working population is weak and unorganized and they are forced to work for these minimum wages because of health problems, lack of education or lack of skills.
The only way that such workers can have their needs adequately taken care of when from time to time the cost of living goes up, as has been the case during the past five years since this government came into office-18 per cent in five years, the greatest increase in any five-year period in Canada's history-is by the senior government in the land giving this matter serious consideration year by year. When the time arrives, as it does each two years in the case of organized workers, the government should increase the minimum wages paid to employees in industries that come under federal jurisdiction. This increase should be related to the negotiated increase on behalf of union employees in unionized industries across Canada.
The way to bring about a satisfactory wage increase for those who work for minimum wages across this country is for the federal government to decide what kind of an increase should be paid and then bring to this house a recommendation for an increase in the minimum wage. I am sure such a measure would be quickly passed by the members of this house.
Once this has been accomplished the Prime Minister should call together the provincial premiers, outline what the federal government has done and urge as strongly as possible that the provincial governments should follow suit. This is the only way that the weak and unorganized workers of this country can receive an adequate wage so as not to fall within the realm of poverty, the position in which one-fifth of the workers in this country find themselves at the present time.
We in this house have never shown any reluctance to increase our own wages. A few years ago we in fact doubled our wages. We increased our wages from $8,000 and $2,000 expenses per year to $12,000 and $6,000 expenses per year. This in fact doubled the wage we received at that time. There was no reluctance on the part of any member of this house or on the part of any government member in suggesting that these wages should be increased. Let me add that there is apparently no reluctance on the part of the government, when Liberal members are defeated, immediately to give them good jobs in various parts of the country so that they will not suffer.

September 20, 1968
The Address-Mr. Hees
It is incumbent upon us at this time to look very carefully at the needs of those in this country who look to us for help, particularly when one-fifth of our working population is living in conditions of poverty. It would not cost the taxpayers of the federal or provincial governments one cent to increase these minimum wages. Such action would simply require the employers who pay minimum wages to pay those who work for them a living wage. There may be some who will say that if we do that we will automatically cause an increase in the cost of goods and services provided by those industries which employ people at minimum wages. I am sure that every member of this house will agree that no Canadian has the right to receive cheap goods or cheap services as a result of paying inadequate wages to that one-fifth of our working population who must then live in poverty.
The Prime Minister has agreed with the report of the Economic Council of Canada and its statement that poverty in this country is a national disgrace. The Prime Minister had this to say about poverty as recorded on page 68 of Hansard:
-we must define, with as much clarity as possible, the essential components of a minimum standard for satisfactory living-not a subsistence standard but one which allows for dignity and decency.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
The Prime Minister also said at another point that they did not need the report of the Economic Council to make them aware of the poverty because they had known about it for a long time. In other words the knowledge about poverty which the Economic Council of Canada made available to Canadians was in the hands of the government and the Prime Minister a long time ago. I am sure, judging by his remarks in this regard, that he knew all about this situation when he became the leader of the government five months ago. Therefore he had adequate opportunity to prepare a practical program for combatting poverty in this country.
With this background I had great hopes that the Prime Minister would tell us what steps he intended to take immediately to make it possible to eradicate poverty in Canada. It was with this hope that I asked him the following question in the House of Commons on Friday last. The question is recorded in Hansard at page 16 and reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a question to the right hon. Prime Minister. Since the Prime

Minister has stated that he agrees with the finding of the Economic Council of Canada that poverty in Canada is a national disgrace, and since the commission has reported that a great deal of this poverty occurs because people who are working are not receiving sufficient wages to enable them to bring up their families in decency and reasonable comfort, do the Prime Minister and the government intend in the very near future to increase the minimum wage as it applies to industries under federal jurisdiction, particularly as this would be an incentive or an example to the provincial governments?
This question came as quite a surprise to the Prime Minister, judging by his answer, because he obviously had not given any thought to such a suggestion and passed the buck to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey). The Minister of Labour, as could be seen by his hesitation in answering the question, was equally taken aback and answered as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Labour is always conscious-
Then there was a long pause.
-of the needs of the working man in this country, and will give consideration to the suggestion of the hon. member.
Members of this house know perfectly well that when a minister of this government tells you a matter is under consideration it means it is something he has not thought about. He feels it would not be wise to refuse to do it but he really has no intention of ever doing anything about it. I tell the 106 new members of the house never to become carried away when a minister tells them he will give their suggestions consideration, because it means that as far as the minister is concerned the suggestion is dead.
I think the Minister of Labour did mean what he said. I believe he would like to do this because he is a humane man who has had great experience with the working people of this country and realizes the need for increasing minimum wages at this time to make it possible for the 4,200,000 people living in poverty to rise above the poverty line. I believe he would like to raise the minimum wage paid to workers in industries under federal jurisdiction. But he will not be allowed to do so because, in his next answer to me, the Prime Minister laid down the party line for action in this regard. Mr. Speaker, you and I know that the members of this cabinet not only are not allowed to speak outside cabinet but I am told they are not even allowed to speak inside cabinet.

speechtext:
Oh, oh.
September 20, 1968

The Address-Mr. Hees

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is only one speaker in cabinet, the Prime Minister, and the 27 little helpers he has for window-dressing are becoming known as the silent 27. Therefore the idea of raising the minimum wage paid to workers in industries under federal jurisdiction will not be considered by this government. I then asked the Prime Minister this supplementary question:
Does the Prime Minister in the very near future intend to call a conference with the provincial premiers to discuss this very vital problem?
His answer was:
The question asked by the hon. member is one relating to wages, costs, prices and incomes.
Now here comes the party line. This is the policy of the Liberal government for combatting inflation. I remind hon. members that this is the government that pledged itself to instituting the just society. The Prime Minister continued his answer in this way:
Our attack seeks to ensure that inflation will be curtailed in Canada. We believe this will be the best attack on the problem.
There it is. It is very easy to understand; there are no complications. That is the plan laid down by no less a person than the Prime Minister. I have no objection and nobody in Canada, of course, could have any objection to the Prime Minister saying that the government is going to take steps to curtail inflation. Heaven knows, inflation needs to be curtailed by the government because they are responsible for the greatest inflation this country has ever known.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

September 20, 1968
The Address

Mr. Hees
per cent increases. Those who are well organized and strong get just about anything they want because of the fact they are organized and strong, and those who are weak and are forced to work for minimum wages in unorganized industries in various parts of this country, those who cannot bring economic pressure to bear on the government, are told that even though there has been a 12 per cent increase in the cost of living since they last received a raise in 1965, the government will not give them an increase now and will not even give them any indication that they will ever get one at any time in the future. Because these people are weak and cannot bring force to bear on the government, they will get nothing.
I asked the Prime Minister whether he would consider raising the minimum wage and he said no. He said, "our approach, which we think is a far better one, will be to curtail inflation". Therefore he will try to allow inflation to increase at somewhere between 2 and 3J per cent per year.
We have now seen what this government's attitude is toward the weak. This is the attitude of the Prime Minister who said he will bring in a just society. It has been made very clear that this government's compassion toward its fellow Canadians is in direct proportion to their strength. If you are strong you get plenty of action from this government, but if you are weak you get absolutely nothing. That is what the Prime Minister said in effect when he laid down his policy for dealing with poverty in this country. The Prime Minister said he is not willing to take the necessary steps to eradicate poverty in our midst. He said he is willing to try to stop it from increasing at too fast a rate, and what he will do is to make sure inflation increases no more than between 2 and 3J per cent a year.
It is clear that the just society about which the Prime Minister spoke all across Canada, at shopping plazas and on television and radio, will have a built-in poverty which will increase year by year. Not only will it not disappear but it will not decrease; in fact it will increase. This is the kind of just society about which the Prime Minister has been talking for the last six months. This is the kind of plan he is putting forward. This is his idea of compassion for those who are weak. He says in effect that if you are strong you get what you want because you are strong, but if you are weak, you get nothing. That is this man's idea of compassion, decency and consideration for his fellow human beings, for

the 4,200,000 who are living in a state of poverty at the present time. It is very clear that the just society about which the Prime Minister spoke is nothing more than a slogan to win elections.
We all heard him talk about the just society all across the country and we could feel his heart bleeding for those poor people who are subjugated to a state of poverty. We could just see the blood that poured out of his heart running all over the place. This is the man who says he will give Canadians a better deal, a more humane deal, the man who claims he is compassionate toward those who cannot look after themselves. Perhaps this man will bring in some constitutional reforms, which are sorely needed, but I can tell you that those 4,200,000 people-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to join in the unanimous chorus of congratulations to you, sir, on your re-election to your high and important office and also couple with that my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address in reply. As you know, at the opening of the last session I was given the honour of moving the address in reply, and I can appreciate fully
September 20, 1968

The Address-Mr. Jamieson
what an important milestone it is in the life of any new parliamentarian.
I have been impressed by the vigour and the degree of participation in this debate, by the vigour more this morning than on previous occasions, and I must say that I find myself on all fours with the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the comments he made the other day on his birthday. Since I entered this house I have been constantly aware of the peculiar kind of kinship that exists among all of us who have chosen this road of public service and which prevails even despite our party loyalties and our sometimes strongly held partisan feelings. I believe that the level of activity in this debate is a good omen, and I hope that on all important matters hon. members, regardless of where they happen to sit in this house, will exercise their best and most objective judgment.
I want to say a word about the speeches made by the leaders of the three parties in this house on the opposite side. I was most impressed with the contribution of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield). As I listened to him and noted the barbs being flung in our direction I felt somewhat like the missionary who, describing an occasion when he was nailed to a tree by the spears of savage natives, was asked if it hurt and replied, "only when I laughed."
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
In the case of the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis), the impression is growing on me that the most appropriate title for this worthy gentleman, and I am sure he will not mind my saying so, is that he has become the smiling cobra of the commons. He has a benign, quiet and friendly approach right up to the very instant before he strikes. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that he has long been, as he well knows, one of my favourite debaters. I am pleased to say, too, that he is one of my close friends. When I refer to his contribution to the debate I can do so best by paraphrasing the familiar expression that, where he is concerned, when attack is inevitable I am quite content to relax and enjoy it.
In so far as the hon. member for Temis-camingue (Mr. Caouette) is concerned, he must surely be a most unusual member of this house. I noted during his contribution to the debate that there were a great many English speaking members of the house who appeared to be understanding everything he was saying without the aid of translation. I feel that he is demonstrating more and more
that an understanding of the language is not always necessary for effective communication. If he would not mind, I would even suggest that perhaps he would be a worthy subject for study by the commission on bilingualism and biculturalism because in his person we may have a solution to many of the serious problems of communication.
Having made these quite sincere statements to the gentlemen opposite, I find it a little bit difficult now to make any criticisms.

speechtext: Now, how do you insult?

speechtext:
Exactly; I do not propose to spend too much time in any essentially negative approach. These three gentlemen, having criticized the Speech from the Throne for its lack of newness and imagination, themselves trotted out all the standard cliches. I suppose if one went back over the last several sessions of this house one could find some similarity in the rebuttals of the opposition leaders. One could really say, therefore, there is nothing of any significance or what I might describe as constructive criticism in what has been said. It may be argued that this is not the role of the opposition.
I should like to turn for a moment to the problems of Newfoundland, but I shall not deal with them in any narrow perspective. I would have to say that those members from my own province who have spoken have adopted much the same approach. I give them the fullest possible marks for sincerity and for being deeply conscientious about the problems of the Atlantic region. They are, like me, first and foremost Newfoundlanders. In dealing with some of the comments that have been made about our approach to the question of regional disparity, I hope I can do so in a constructive manner, without being overly critical or generating what I regard as the useless antagonisms that have on many occasions in the past made it difficult to achieve any meaningful advances.
Let me emphasize once again that I think the immediate importance of the problems of regional disparity are not exclusively those of Newfoundland. However, I believe that by examining what has been happening in that island province, where we have made mistakes and where some of the programs that have been implemented over the years have been failures, it should be possible, as the Speech from the Throne suggests and as some hon. members on the opposite side have suggested, for us to take a hard look at the whole picture. We should be examining the
280	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Jamieson possibility of integrating all the different schemes that have been devised on an ad hoc basis over the years. We should be bringing these programs into some kind of focus which will result in permanent advancement and improvement.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has said that the government, and I presume he was going back to 1949, has been guilty of shameful neglect of the problems of Newfoundland and the Atlantic region. Let me emphasize that I am not going to argue his statement of conditions that exist. I do suggest, however, that the charge of shameful neglect is not one that can stand on all fours with the facts of the case. I doubt very much that he can argue too strongly against my proposition because he was a supporter of a government which did a great deal, I am ready to concede, for the Atlantic region. Since that time other programs have been implemented and have been added to those which were introduced in those years and previously. I believe, therefore, that the sum total of aid that has been advanced to the Atlantic region, in the case of Newfoundland since 1949, is really quite impressive.
One has only to look, for example, at the numerous benefits to our province that have resulted from the completion of the trans-Canada highway at a very great cost. One has only to total all the contributions that have been made over the years, one way and another, to bolster and support the fishing industry. There have been any number of other projects, some of general application to all Canadians all over this nation, and others that have applied to the Atlantic area alone or even to Newfoundland expressly. The truth of the matter is that in the case of Newfoundland, since 1949 right through until now, nearly 20 years, the real indictment of these programs, the real indictment of administrations at the federal level whatever their party colouration, is that they have not succeeded, despite these fantastic expenditures relatively speaking, in curing the essential and basic problems.
A case in point is one which my hon. friends opposite have talked about in this house and outside on a number of occasions. It is something which will be almost totally foreign, I believe, to other parts of the nation except Newfoundland and the Atlantic region.
I refer to the salt subsidy program. I should like to dwell on this for a moment because it is illustrative, it seems to me, of the kind of thing that we ought not to be doing and perhaps ought not to have been doing over the

DEBATES	September 20, 1968
past number of years. This salt subsidy program is a federal contribution to a particular provincial problem, a regional problem. The program was introduced for one year 15 years ago to deal with a specific and unique development within the fishing industry. It was clearly stated at that time, and everyone understood, that it was not to be an ongoing program. Yet 15 years later, the program is still in existence because when we arrived at each new fall season and made an assessment of the fishing season someone said that was not the year to cancel it. The program was designed for a very special purpose and in fact it was really disguised welfare. It has been larded on year after year for a period of 15 years.
We have expended, I suppose, in excess of $10 million on this program in a period of 15 years. I do not know the exact figure without looking up the records but it must be in that neighbourhood. This amount has been paid out in dribs and drabs over the years, so that after 15 years we find hon. gentlemen opposite able to claim that the cancellation of the program amounts to a near death blow to Newfoundland and the Atlantic provinces' fishing industry. Even conceding the seriousness of the withdrawal for a moment, the really significant point is that the amount involved here, if my hon. friends are right and it makes the difference between security and the lack of it for the Newfoundland fisherman, is not much more than $350,000.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is a great deal of money.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's East stated that there were about 150,000 people engaged in the Newfoundland fishing industry. I suggest that may be something of an exaggeration, but that is beside the point. If $350,000 spread over a group of
150,000	people, either directly or indirectly, is going to have such an effect, it is clearly indicative of the fact the program has failed. I say, therefore, we must look quickly at the alternative. I quite agree it is not enough simply to carve off programs that are demonstrably inefficient. You have to provide alternatives. I do say to those gentlemen, and to members in this house in general, that it serves no useful purpose to continue with this kind of dribs and drabs contribution when after 15 years we find the program is not really making a significant contribution to the protection or improvement of the fishing industry.
September 20, 1968

There are two other aspects of the program that are wrong that I should like to mention.
I merely use this example to illustrate once again why it is so important that we have, as the throne speech suggests, a detailed reexamination of a great many programs. One of the difficulties or shortcomings of the salt rebate program is that the more fish a man catches the more salt he is going to use. The more salt he uses, the greater the rebate he is going to receive. The conclusion is surely obvious, therefore, that the man who needs it least gets the largest rebate in a great many cases because he does have a substantial catch to sell.
The second point is that because of the structure of the program, which was set up on an interim one year basis, no one has really had the courage to say, surely we should halt this subsidy. The third point is that a very substantial part of the moneys given under this program, the withdrawal of which hon. gentlemen call a death blow, goes to the business community. While I am not suggesting for one moment that the fishing trade or business community is not entitled to consideration, let me assure you, gentlemen, that my heart is not bleeding for those people. If $500,000 or $600,000 or $700,000 is going to be given to the Newfoundland fisheries, then let it go to the primary producers, particularly in this case and indeed in many other cases as well.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
I have taken a fair amount of time to discuss this matter, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is typical of the sort of band-aid solutions, as I have called them, applied by successive governments. If hon. gentlemen opposite are being critical of this administration, then let us have the same kind of criticism made of those who were in office up until 1963.
I am surprised, Mr. Speaker, and in fact a little puzzled, by the extent to which my hon. friends opposite from Newfoundland made the welkin ring over the cancellation of the winter works program. Here again is another of those examples of why we need to rethink these schemes. If these hon. gentlemen opposite had bothered to look at the details and the facts that are readily available to them, they would have discovered that in the last year of this program, that is, the 1967-68 season, out of an amount in excess of $20 million provided from federal funds for this program the absolute maximum total of funds spent in Newfoundland was $135,000. This, Mr. Speaker, out of more than $20 million.

The Address-Mr. Jamieson
Furthermore, if they observe how the rest of the money was spent they might also discover that the largest proportion of it went into the large metropolitan areas. I am prepared to concede that the big cities do have a different kind of problem, and my argument, therefore, at this point is not whether the winter works program was a good idea. But in the case of Newfoundland it is clearly evident that it was not worth the powder to blow it to Hades-$135,000 expended, spread over a period of five or six months. For the most part the municipalities merely shifted necessary works from one month to another, thus in totality generating no new employment at all.
Another defect in the program, if one takes a look at it as a regional development concept, is that the smaller the municipality, the less the funds for it to meet its share of the over-all expenditure. If hon. members would like to look at the figures they would find that in one place after another in Newfoundland amounts of $1,000 or $500 were spent, all small amounts with the possible exception of the city of St. John's. But essentially the weakness of the program was our inability to take advantage of it because of the failure on the part of the municipalities to find their share of the money.
It seems to me that when we talk of Newfoundland and of Atlantic Canada it is simple, easy and routine to get up and ask why we do not put more money into a project here or a project there, or to damn and criticize the government when it withdraws programs such as those I have mentioned. For Newfoundland and I suspect for all of Atlantic Canada-and it may be equally true in other non-urban regions of the country-the real necessity now is to examine all of the things that are being done, because in total they are most impressive.
As the throne speech suggests, Mr. Speaker, we must make some hard decisions both at this level and at the provincial level. We must examine the priorities that are available to us. Here again there is no better example of this than another of those emotion charged issues in which Newfoundlanders appear to delight. I refer to the decision to withdraw the Canadian National Railways passenger service in Newfoundland. This is something that we in Newfoundland must face, Mr. Speaker, and I think this provides a good example. There is no question, even in the minds of those who wish to see the railway retained, that this subsidy or operating loss will go even higher. In all of this, Mr. Speaker, I am qualifying what I say by emphasizing my own contention, which is well known to gentlemen opposite, that should it become a question of abandonment the personnel involved must be completely and totally protected. We should not permit them to become the victims of some technological change. So as I say, Mr. Speaker, we have these choices to make.
Instead of having coastal boats of this sort and various heavily subsidized means of transportation, there is no doubt in my mind that we must look much harder than we have up to now, not only in Newfoundland but in many other places, at the process of centralization. It is very easy on a warm summer's afternoon to become ecstatic about the tranquil beauty of some isolated community and the rustic charm of some settlement which can be reached only by a pleasant ocean voyage over a calm sea. I am guilty of this kind of romanticizing myself, and indeed from time to time have been regretful of the pressures of modern society which appear, at least, to make this kind of livelihood no longer viable. However, it would be, and is in the case of some hon. members and others, the most shameful form of exploitation to suggest to residents of many of these isolated communities that in some way or other through government aid, and if we were big-hearted enough, we might provide them with the same level of amenities that society is now able to offer larger and more accessible areas. It simply cannot be done, Mr. Speaker.

When talking about Newfoundland we must abandon some popular notions. We must abandon the approach of going to 25, 30 or 40 families and saying to them, "You stay here; this is where you belong." it is." The fact of the matter is that the people in these Atlantic communities who supposedly are leading a tranquil existence, a pleasant life, and who are being uprooted and driven off into the industrial world have, or the great majority of them have, a sordid 100-year or more history of sadness, privation and even death which has resulted from their isolation.
Those who are against the present trend and who criticize government activity in this field are oblivious of the real facts. Within a matter of time the majority of these isolated communities will phase out of their own accord. When 7,000, 8,000 or 9,000 young people every year attend university, high school, vocational school or other centres of higher learning and when in Newfoundland, as in other parts of Canada, educational opportunities have become so greatly improved, one cannot blame our young people for not going back to the settlements from which they originated. It is only a matter of time before our communities phase themselves out. Even if we say to these people, "Stay, we will do all we can for you", and even if we encourage them to stay by providing what limited improvements are possible in the kinds of geographically isolated regions they live in, even then the drift toward centralization is irresistible. Instead of adopting this reactionary approach, Mr. Speaker, is it not more responsible to do everything possible to help our young people establish themselves and to bring them out of this isolation in a way that will ensure, at least, that they have a reasonable chance?
Where there have been failures-and I readily concede that there have been failures in some aspects of the centralization program -they have arisen because there has not been enough integration of the plan. Too vividly have we seen one side of the equation, the necessity to get them out, and we have not been sufficiently concerned with the sociological problems which have arisen. It is not enough to give a man a home or a few thousand dollars in order to move him to a more productive area. There are many other human problems of one kind or another which must be considered. In this regard I admit there have been difficulties.
On balance, the great majority of those who have moved under the centralization program are glad they did. I should like to take some of my colleagues on the opposition side who have different views and in their company talk to some of these people and ask

Therefore I can only say with deep sincerity and conviction that I am profoundly grateful for this unprecedented honour and I shall do my utmost to become a worthy member of parliament under the leadership of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), who has continually encouraged and counselled me, and the guidance of many hon. members on both sides of this house who have expressed an interest in my political career, sanctioned, I fervently pray, by Him without whom all goals are unattainable.
September 20, 1968

I am privileged to say that I was born in Ontario, the province of opportunity, the province to which many people in Canada look for leadership because it has progressed so dynamically, welcoming all peoples, regardless of race, creed or colour, desirous of contributing to its phenomenal growth and sharing its wealth and the good life. Within that province is the city in which I live, the city that has adopted me and propelled me with jet-like propulsion to the House of Commons.
In view of the time allotted to me, and because I would like to make some observations on other matters, I cannot recite a complete and adequate picture of the city of Hamilton, or in fact my riding of Hamilton West, one of four in the city that escaped Trudeaumania, much to the disbelief and bewilderment of the Grits. In any event, I find it necessary to speak about some of the important points of Hamilton because, as I understand it, a member is likely not to have another opportunity.
I would like to commence by pointing out to you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members that Hamilton had another first in the person of Hon. Ellen Fairclough, Canada's first woman cabinet member, who no doubt is warmly remembered by many hon. members because of her outstanding contribution to this house.

To her I owe much, and I shall continue to rely on her wisdom and experience.
This city of almost 300,000 in population is the steel centre of Canada, producing more than one half of Canada's steel. It is interesting to note that iron and steel industry sales all across Canada make up approximately 2.7 per cent of the gross national product, therefore being even greater than wheat which is 1.7 per cent.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
Because of the importance of this industry to our economy, Canada's principal basic steel producers, among which the Hamilton steel industry plays an important role, are of course very interested in the new anti-dumping code agreed to by Canada in the recent General Agreement of Tariffs and Trade. Mr. Speaker, you will recall that something was said on this subject this morning. Industry regards dumping as a serious problem and is justifiably concerned about the potential loss of domestic markets to foreign competition at
The Address-Mr. Alexander dump prices arising from Canada's acceptance of article VI of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
Industry recognizes that competition on a fair trade basis is customary and of course challenging. However, competition at less than fair market value is disturbing and cannot be considered fair. In fact it may result in irreparable damage to the domestic industry and to the economy. It is suggested that the onus of preventing undue disruption from dumping into the domestic market rests completely on the importing country. Therefore I strongly urge that the government be very aware of the dangers of dumping, and in enacting any laws to bring the anti-dumping agreement into effect deep consideration and attention should be given to the scope of the legislation and the form of administration of the law because Hamilton, and indeed Canada, neither want nor can afford harmful effects on the economy.
Although steel plays a great role in the life of Hamilton, the manufacturing of machinery, electrical goods, rubber, chemicals and textiles also mean a livelihood for many Hamiltonians. Hamilton can further boast of the port of Hamilton which has a 10-mile waterfront providing three miles of berthing space. It is a port of call for 50 shipping lines and it has agencies with services to and from 100 world ports. Present trends suggest that the port will become an increasingly important seaport gateway through which an ever-growing volume of exports and imports will be shipped, thereby allowing it to continue to break records in terms of tonnage moved. In this connection may I remind the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) that notwithstanding the fact that in a democracy one can expect strikes, Hamilton would take issue with him in the event there was a prolonged strike in this area.
One cannot speak of Hamilton without reference to McMaster University, my alma mater, which has attracted and continues to attract students from all over the world who seek excellence in graduate and post-graduate studies. It is worth while mentioning that Hamilton's rock garden because of its floral display has received international acclaim. May I also point out, if anyone is in doubt, that Hamilton still has faith in the Hamilton Tiger Cats football team.
The city of Hamilton is progressing with an urban renewal program including a civic square, and Hamiltonians continue to expect, and in fact deserve, immediate, decisive and
290	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Alexander continued government leadership in that regard.
Of some concern to Hamilton at the present time are its plans for a cultural centre-the Hamilton theatre auditorium. Toward this end may I say that the people of Hamilton have made and met their financial commitments; the province of Ontario has made and is prepared to honour its commitment, and we now look to this government to become involved pursuant to the many requests made upon it so that a firm and early commitment may be expected. It is hoped that the government is as enthusiastic about receiving briefs and submissions on this project as are the Hamiltonians in presenting them.
Hamilton is no different from any other large city. Of course it has its urban problems. Hamiltonians also are very concerned about housing, unemployment, inflation, air and water pollution, lack of mortgage moneys, high interest rates, and lack of serviced land. These are the areas to which priority should be directed.
Hamiltonians, and indeed all Canadians, believed that the Speech from the Throne would indicate solutions to these problems with greater clarity as related to the just society, a phrase without definition and an election slogan that has frustrated and confused many. Canadians want solutions to the many social and economic problems which burden this nation. They want them now, and they will not be satisfied with tokenism and expression of intentions for the future.
It is not unreasonable to conclude that because the Prime Minister spoke of the just society on the hustings and said, "follow me, give me a majority", Canadians had the right to expect and believe that this government would present to them a dynamic, inspiring and moving political manifesto in the speech from the throne. I can remember the arrival of the Prime Minister in Hamilton and I can remember reading about him and his smile when he said "follow me" and they walked. Then he became famous for that which many of us younger ones would want to be famous and for which we feel some jealousy. The women said, "where do we go?" He said, "follow me", and they walked.
Now it is implied that the government did not have to give this country leadership or direction in the speech from the throne. Apparently, in the mind of the government, this conclusion was unreasonable on the part of the people and reached without justification, much to the dismay and disappointment of

DEBATES	September 20, 1968
many Canadians. I too am disappointed and in total disagreement with the utterances of many political experts who believe that it is inevitable that the speech from the throne should be dull, uninspiring and empty. Such speeches are not and never will be accepted. This is 1968, the jet propelled age and not the days of the horse and buggy.
As a result of their disappointment, Canadians have changed. I say that sincerely. They are no longer uninformed, naive and gullible. At this time an expression comes to my mind which was continually referred to by the late Dr. Martin Luther King in speeches in which he quoted the ungrammatical truths of an old preacher among which was the following; "We ain't what we oughta be, we ain't what we could be, we ain't what we should be, but thank God we ain't what we was." I say to the government: take heed and wake up before it is too late.
Mr. Speaker, since coming to this house I have become more and more aware of the tremendous responsibilities of a member of parliament. He must grapple conscientiously and diligently with the many problems which face this nation. He must find with expediency the solutions to them. He must be concerned about the quality of life being experienced by all Canadians. He must create with enthusiasm and confidence a climate of proper direction to ensure the realization of our ultimate goal, that of a greater Canada in which we can all pray, live, work and play harmoniously while enjoying the fruits of full economic development. To these ends I dedicate my strength and my abilities and in this dedication my thoughts are directed toward many people in Canada about whom I and my constituents in Hamilton West are concerned.
We are concerned about the fact that four million people live in poverty. We are concerned about the fact that the dream of owning one's home has apparently become an impossible dream under this administration. We are concerned about the fact that unemployment is at the unwarranted high level of more than 400,000. We are concerned about the reliance on welfare by many. We are concerned about the fact that because of inflation the pensioners, the aged, the disabled and those on fixed incomes have very little purchasing power.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Does this government have the solutions to these basic problems that face this nation? If
September 20, 1968

they have let them kindly advise the country, because the country is waiting for the answers. I say to this government, this is the time to show greater evidence of its concern. This is unquestionably a time for reassessment, a time for awakening. This is a time for reflection on the past only to better enable us to determine the guide lines and direction that positive action for the immediate future must take, particularly in relation to economic development, research and technology. We would then be in a more favourable position to solve these problems.
It seems to me that in a just society it should be the continuing responsibility of this government to be constantly aware of and concerned about the degree of the quality of life that each and every Canadian is experiencing. If there is any disparity, no matter how little, then the government should immediately set itself to reducing it, thereby assuring that each and every individual can live a full productive life and become in fact an essential part of the mainstream of Canadian life for the betterment of all Canadians.
I should like to move now, Mr. Speaker, to another topic. I am the first black man elected to the House of Commons. This results from the fact that many Hamiltonians have accepted as a way of life a simple truism expressed by Adele Florence Corey long ago. She said that men should be judged not by the colour of their skin nor by the way they fight, love or sin, nor by the gods they serve or vintage they drink, but by the quality of thoughts they think. How simple that statement is, but how unacceptable to many. Yet, if this way of life is not accepted, speak not to me of the Bill of Rights; speak not to me of democracy; speak not to me of the brotherhood of man or the fatherhood of God, because this then becomes hypocrisy. The black man also desires a place in the mainstream of life and because of this we read of his struggle, and struggle he must.
Listen to what Frederick Douglas, that great abolitionist, said back in 1857 about struggle. He said;
The whole history of the progress of human liberty shows that all concessions yet made to her august claims have been born of earnest struggle. If there is no struggle, there is no progress. Those who profess freedom yet deprecate struggle are men who want crops without ploughing up the ground; they want rain without thunder and lightning. Power concedes nothing without a demand.
The Address-Mr. Haidasz
I look at the government.
It never did and it never will. Men may not get all they pay for in this world, but they must certainly pay for all they get.
The negro has to struggle. Some say I have it made. Let me, standing here, be no indication that all negroes in Canada have it made. Let me say this: the negro has awakened with a new soul. He knows he is somebody. He is Thurgoode Marshall, Supreme Court Justice; he is Dr. Ralph Bunche, diplomat extraordinaire. He is Carl Stokes, mayor of Cleveland. He is Dr. Martin Luther King, whose passive resistance movement has changed the nature of the thinking of the whole free world. He is Leonard Braithwaite who, even though a Liberal, sits at Queens Park in Toronto. He is the high commissioners and ambassadors we see here in Ottawa.
This is an impressive list, I know, but I wonder how many men of such calibre we have lost because of the deliberate rejection of people because of colour? I am not the spokesman for the negro; that honour has not been given to me. Do not let me ever give anyone that impression. However, I want the record to show that I accept the responsibility for speaking for him and all others in this great nation who feel that they are the subjects of discrimination because of race, creed or colour.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would say that our role in the building of the "just society", if it is to become a reality, is that we as parliamentarians must be involved with the hopes, the fears, the disappointments, legitimate aspirations and despair of each and every Canadian, ever mindful that involvement demands commitment in terms of actions and deeds, rather than words only.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne of the first session of this parliament, I am eager to congratulate you on your re-election as Speaker of the house and to wish you every success in the performance of your heavy duties.
I also wish to congratulate the Deputy Speaker and the Deputy Chairman of committees (Messrs. Faulkner and Bechard) on their appointment.
I wish to add as well my congratulations to those that have already been made to the hon.
September 20, 1968

The Address-Mr. Haidasz member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin), who has been chosen to move the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. The depth of his thoughts and the enthusiasm with which he expressed them assure us that he will bring a worthy contribution to the house proceedings.
I also want to congratulate the member for Kamloops-Caribou (Mr. Marchand), the first member of Indian origin to sit in this house and the mover of the address in reply. I salute his arrival in the house, as I salute that of the member who has just finished his speech. His presence in this house, as well as his special knowledge, will no doubt help us to better understand the problems of the minorities of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in joining my colleagues and my electors in congratulating the right honourable Prime Minister on his victory and that of the Liberal party in the general election of June 25. His wish for a just society, as well as the devotion and the courage with which he pursues that goal, is welcomed with great satisfaction and enthusiasm by my electors and, doubtless by all the citizens of Canada. I am particularly pleased to hear his statements and especially to read in the Speech from the Throne that constitutional reforms are the best guarantee of Canadian unity.
Our most important duty during this parliament is to strengthen national unity. Moreover, the Canadian charter of human rights must ensure to all our citizens the protection of fundamental liberties.
I wish also to thank the right hon. Prime Minister for the honour he extended to me by calling me to the office of Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). I shall endeavour to fulfil my duties to the best of my abilities and I may add that I am very pleased to try and help the ministers, all the members and the Canadian people at this critical hour.
With the experience he has, the minister quite obviously understands the daily problems of Canadians and judging by the manner I have seen this department work since it has been his responsibility, I am convinced that the Canadian consumers are already being helped and will be helped further in the future.
Mr. Speaker, in the discharge of my duties, I want also to express my gratitude to the electors of Parkdale for having elected me as 
their representative in this house. I hope that I will, at all times, serve loyally and devotedly my constituents and my fellow-citizens.
Parkdale constituency, which is situated in the southwest area of Toronto, is almost a miniature replica of a cosmopolitan centre. Besides the Anglo-Saxon and French-Canadi-an groups, almost all other ethnic groups live there. As was the case for many of our ancestors, many of my constituents immigrated here to start a new life. Some came with a spirit of adventure; others were in quest of freedom. Coming to Canada in large numbers, thanks to a judicious immigration policy of the Liberal party, they have found freedom and a better life in this country. They are proud of the traditions of our country and anxious to participate in its development. A great many of them have contributed to a large extent to our economy as labourers, teachers, doctors, lawyers, engineers, missionaries, artists, etc.
During May last, the right honourable Prime Minister honoured us by presiding at a ceremony and unveiling a monument, in Toronto, commemorating Sir Casimir Stanislas Gzowski, one of the first Polish immigrants that settled in Toronto. On account of his services to Canada as an engineer and a statesman, he was knighted by Queen Victoria, in 1890.
Mr. Speaker, the immigrants constitute an invaluable asset for the future of Canada. The great amount of respect shown by my constituents toward our free and democratic way of life is very enlightening. They are firmly decided not to lose the freedom they have found in this country. Hence, they have an uncompromising desire to help those nations that have lost their freedom.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)

Among my constituents who, especially at this time, have demonstrated, and rightly so, a grave concern for freedom and basic human rights, a concern shared, I hope, by all Canadians, are those of Czech and Slovak origins. The aborting of the long awaited liberalization process in Czechoslovakia by the Soviet led invasion of that unfortunate country on August 20 shocked our citizens and indeed the people of the free world as well as many citizens in countries behind the iron curtain. This blow to freedom has marred the world's celebration of human rights year. The General Assembly of the United Nations
September 20, 1968

declared 1968 human rights year to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the declaration of human rights. I am sure we would all like to express the hope, Mr. Speaker, that before the end of this unfortunate year basic freedoms and human rights will be returned to the people of Czechoslovakia.
While attending the international congress of gastroenterology held in Prague in mid-July of this year I had the opportunity of not only visiting and admiring the 1,000 year old historical evidence of Christianity and western civilization, but also the privilege of meeting and speaking with people from all walks of life in that geographically small but rich and beautiful country of Czechoslovakia.
It was evident that Czechs and Slovaks awaited with a curious and patient expectation the beginnings of basic freedoms and human rights, and yearned for an economic growth that would benefit the common working man. But their hopes were short lived. On August 20 the cold harshness of the imperialistic designs of a totalitarian state extinguished the fire of freedom in Czechoslovakia. I believe, however, that the intense desire of the defiant people of that country to be free to determine their own destiny will never be extinguished.
The Canadian government, both at home and abroad, protested against the invasion of Czechoslovakia. At the United Nations Security Council emergency session the distinguished and able Canadian representative immediately voiced Canada's protest by cosponsoring a resolution condemning the Soviet intervention, and then initiated a second resolution which sought to ensure the release and safety of the leaders of Czechoslovakia. In Ottawa, following an emergency session of cabinet, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) stated unequivocally Canada's protest and voiced our indignation.
In Toronto at a public protest rally, I read on behalf of the Secretary of State for External Affairs a special message which condemned the Soviet led invasion of Czechoslovakia. The message also stated that the Canadian government had unequivocally condemned this use of force and called for the immediate end of the Soviet occupation.
By its actions the U.S.S.R. had chosen brutally to ignore the most basic principle of international law and two of the cardinal principles of the United Nations charter; that of the sovereign equality of states, and the obligation that states must refrain in their international relations from the use of force
The Address-Mr. Haidasz against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. The Canadian government has been in the forefront of the efforts at the United Nations to aid the people of Czechoslovakia. Canada does not condone the occupation of Czechoslovakia nor the illegal and unjustified intervention of the U.S.S.R.
The special message of the Secretary of State for External Affairs also stated that an agreement reached under duress resulting from military occupation and this mode of resolving difficulties between states is completely repugnant to the Canadian government. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government showed its compassion in dealing with the consequences of the Czechoslovak tragedy. Already Canada has offered a new home and emergency financial assistance to the nearly 500 refugees from Czechoslovakia. This is an enviable record which I do not think has been surpassed to this date by any other government outside Vienna. It is to the credit of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen), with the co-operation of his cabinet colleagues and the efficient work of his officials, that Canada has provided such humanitarian treatment to these refugees.
May I encourage the minister to continue his efforts and also suggest to him that he add to the special Canadian team recently sent to Vienna more departmental officials and also representatives from Czech and Slovak national organizations in Canada. Such a move, I believe, is desirable in view of yesterday's Reuters press report from Munich that according to the international rescue committee there are more than 30,000 refugees from Czechoslovakia homeless in various parts of western Europe.
I believe many Canadians are impatiently awaiting the forthcoming session of the general assembly of the United Nations. Perhaps many people are hoping for too much, but, Mr. Speaker, despite its weaknesses, the United Nations is still the best instrument for peace and justice that the world today possesses. In the meantime, Canada should work toward the establishment of an impartial and effective international control agency. Such a body should be empowered to preserve peace and justice by controlling the proliferation of nuclear weapons, negotiating peaceful disputes, advancing human rights and supporting economic development.
294	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Haidasz [DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As the representative of Parkdale I also have deep concern for my constituents who, at the same time, are citizens of the great municipality of metropolitan Toronto. This great city was the first community in the western hemisphere to give political recognition to the metropolitan form of government, which was created by the demands of modern, industrial society. Metropolitan Toronto was legally established in April, 1953, by an act of the Ontario Legislature.
Toronto plays an important role in the development of our entire country, and not just in the development of Ontario. This great municipality, with a population of 1,900,000 persons-the population increases by about
60,000	persons each year-soon will contain nearly 10 per cent of all Canada. A great industrial and educational centre, Toronto is also a major port in the St. Lawrence seaway system; through the port are forwarded domestic and foreign cargoes to almost all parts of the North American continent as well as to many overseas countries.
During this long, hot summer I, with several Liberal colleagues of this house, attended meetings of the city of Toronto redevelopment advisory council, as well as meetings of other public agencies and officials concerning the great redevelopment plan of Toronto's downtown core, the Toronto harbour and the new 50 mile long waterfront, including a new and bold concept for the Canadian National Exhibition grounds. On September 10 the Toronto planning board approved an official and complete 15 year development plan, during which time metropolitan Toronto's population is expected to grow to 3 million people.
Toronto's redevelopment plan includes matters under federal jurisdiction such as transportation, new airports, extended harbour facilities, a post office in central downtown, a radio and television broadcasting centre, a new waterfront and, as I mentioned before, large grounds for the Canadian National Exhibition.
I am happy to see the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) in his seat this afternoon, and I extend to him an invitation to visit Toronto as soon as possible, to see the operations of the central post office. He might also wish to learn of the plan the Toronto planning board has for the relocation of the central post office. At the same time I extend a similar invitation to all other cabinet ministers whose departments have a bearing on this redevelopment plan. It is definitely in the national

DEBATES	September 20, 1968
interest to utilize all our technical know-how and financial resources in order to carry out these redevelopment plans. The people of Toronto need and demand swift action. Federal and provincial co-operation with Toronto officials on these matters will stimulate a great sector of the Canadian economy, provide thousands of new jobs and eventually increase our national revenue.
I submit that further provincial and federal initiatives are indispensible to the improvement of the quality of life in our sprawling urban centres. The problems of slums, poverty, disease, delinquency, crime, inadequate housing, air pollution, contaminated water and traffic congestion will choke our cities and paralyze the entire Canadian economy unless all levels of government plan and act more quickly. All our urban problems which have national implications must be examined thoroughly. The influence of modern environment on Canadian citizens is a major and urgent national issue. In order to cope with these and other environmental problems I suggest to the federal government that we establish a special department of urban and environmental affairs.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say that the government's legislative program has an underlying basic philosophy and an appreciation of the right priorities. It will satisfy many needs and provide better living conditions in our present, complex, modem society. I support and have confidence in this legislative program which, I submit, merits favourable consideration by members on both sides of the house.
